rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The discovery lets the king and his subjects know that resurrection, reward, punishment, and the Hour are certain.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد الملك # ورعيته) (¬1)، أن البعث والثواب والعقاب حق

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: The dispute among the people of that age concerned resurrection; al-Wahidi calls this the likeliest interpretation.
rows.anchor: فالأشبه ما قال عكرمة: (أن أهل ذلك الزمان تنازعوا بالبعث)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their disputed matter was resurrection; the time clause is governed by “We made them known,” meaning God disclosed them as the dispute arose.
rows.anchor: والمراد بقوله: {أمرهم} ما تنازعوا فيه من أمر البعث

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Alternatively, the time clause can depend on “so that they know”: they learned at the time of their dispute.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون منصوبا بقوله: {ليعلموا} أي: ليعلموا في وقت منازعتهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس رواية عطاء
rows.claim: A man sent to buy food showed the youths a coin bearing Decianus's image, and they disputed with him and rejected his account.
rows.anchor: وذلك أن الرجل إذ خرج ليشتري لهم الطعام لما وقف يتنازع، نظروا إلى درهمه

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some say the dispute concerned how long the youths had stayed, but al-Wahidi says this does not fit the clause's syntax unless it is detached as a new command to recall the dispute.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم: (يعني تنازعوا في قدر مكثهم ولبثهم) (¬6)

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some say they disputed their number; al-Wahidi rejects this for the same syntactic reason as the proposed dispute about their duration.
rows.anchor: وقيل: (تنازعوا # في عددهم) (¬1)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another reported view is that the dispute concerned building over the youths and making a mosque; the surrounding words about building support it.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من قال: (هذا التنازع يعود إلى التنازع في البنيان، والمسجد)، يروى هذا عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The proposed building was meant to conceal the youths from people.
rows.anchor: يعني استروهم من الناس، قال ذلك المفسرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Their Lord knows best about them” suggests a dispute over their number, and means that God knows their count; compare the next verse.
rows.anchor: يدل على أنه وقع تنازع في عدتهم، فمعنى: {ربهم أعلم بهم}، أي: بعددهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “their Lord knows best” may be God's own new statement or the words of people arguing about the youths' number.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن هذا من قول الله ابتداء، ويحتمل أنه من قول بعض الناس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Those who prevailed in the matter were believers who did not doubt resurrection.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد المؤمنين الذين لم يشكوا في البعث)

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Exegetes identify those who prevailed as King Theodosius and his companions.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: (هم تندوسيس الملك وأصحابه)

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: The mosque indicates that believers in resurrection prevailed, since mosques belong to believers.
rows.anchor: هذا يدل على أنه لما ظهر أمرهم غلب المؤمنون بالبعث والنشور؛ لأن المساجد للمؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Over them” means placing the structure behind or around them, as when a wall is built around something.
rows.anchor: ومعنى: {عليهم} هاهنا وفي قوله: {ابنوا عليهم بنيانا} أنهم يجعلون وراء ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account says the king built a mosque at the cave entrance and established an annual festival there.
rows.anchor: أن الملك جعل على باب الكهف مسجدا يصلى فيه، وجعل عنده عيدا عظيما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi says the verse is difficult in its apparent wording and arrangement, and that God knows best what it means.
rows.anchor: والآية مشكلة الظاهر والنظم، والله أعلم بما أراد

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The command disciplines the Prophet to qualify a future resolve with God's will: say “if God wills” when promising to do something tomorrow.
rows.anchor: هذا تأديب من الله تعالى لنبيه -عليه السلام-، وأمر له بالاستثناء فيما يعزم بمشيئة الله

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: “Unless God wills” means “unless He intends.”
rows.anchor: قال الفراء في قوله: (إلا أن يشاء الله}: إلا أن يريد الله

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: The particle “an” is accusative: do not say you will act except by God's will; he supplies an implied preposition.
rows.anchor: موضع {أن} نصب، المعنى: لا تقولن إني أفعل إلا بمشيئة الله

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Alternatively, understand an omitted “say”: “unless he says, if God wills”; a short expression can stand for the longer one by indication.
rows.anchor: وقال الأخفش: (أي: إلا أن يقول: إن شاء الله.

rows.speaker: المبرد عن الكسائي والفراء
rows.claim: They likewise supply an omitted verb of saying; deleting it shifts “wills” into the future form.
rows.anchor: روي عن المبرد عن الكسائي والفراء قالا: (المعنى إني فاعل ذلك غدا

rows.speaker: أكثر الناس
rows.claim: Most interpreters take “remember your Lord when you forget” to mean: if you forgot to say “if God wills,” say it when you remember.
rows.anchor: أكثر الناس على أن معناه: إذا نسيت الاستثناء بمشيئة الله تعالى فاذكره، وقله إذا ذكرت

rows.speaker: ابن عباس رواية عطاء
rows.claim: The forgotten qualification may be supplied even after a month.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس رواية عطاء: (يريد الاستثناء ولو بعد شهر)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For a promise without an oath, forgetting the qualification violates the command, but saying it later when remembered removes blame.
rows.anchor: فإذا ذكر أنه كان قد نسي الاستثناء فقاله وضع عنه الحرج

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: If someone forgets “if God wills” after promising to act tomorrow, he should say it when he remembers, even after a day, month, or year.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد بن جبير: (إذا قلت لشيء إنك فاعله غدا

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: When you remember, make the qualification.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو العالية: (إذا ذكرت فاستثن)

rows.speaker: عمرو بن دينار
rows.claim: The qualification remains available whenever the person remembers.
rows.anchor: وقال عمرو بن دينار: (له الاستثناء متى ما ذكر)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These delayed qualifications concern promises without oaths; an oath qualified by a connected “if God wills” is not broken.
rows.anchor: هذا كله فيما يعد من نفسه أن يفعله من غير يمين، فإن حلف ثم استثنى بمشيئة الله متصلا بيمينه

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة عن النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet said that whoever swears and says “if God wills” does not break the oath.
rows.anchor: روى أبو هريرة عن النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم: "من حلف فقال: إن شاء الله

rows.speaker: ابن عمر عن النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet said that a person who swears and says “if God wills” has the choice to act or not.
rows.anchor: وروى ابن عمر عن النبي -صلى الله عليه وسلم- قال: "من حلف على يمين فقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There is no disagreement about a connected qualification; disagreement concerns one separated from the oath.
rows.anchor: ولا خلاف في هذا بين الناس، وإنما الخلاف فيه إذا انقطع الاستثناء عن اليمين

rows.speaker: الحسن عن قتادة
rows.claim: A qualification counts when spoken continuously with the oath and with no intervening speech.
rows.anchor: روى قتادة عن الحسن في الرجل يحلف فيستثني في يمينه قال: (له ثنياه إذا اتصل كلامه

rows.speaker: طاووس
rows.claim: A separated qualification still counts as long as the person remains in the same session.
rows.anchor: وقال طاووس: (له ثنياه ما كان في مجلسه)

rows.speaker: حماد
rows.claim: A qualification kept only in one's mind does not count until one hears oneself say it.
rows.anchor: وعن حماد (¬2) قال: (إن استثنى في نفسه فليس بشيء حتى يسمع نفسه)

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Moving the tongue to articulate the qualification is sufficient.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: (إذا حرك لسانه أجزأ عنه)

rows.speaker: مذهب الشافعي
rows.claim: In the Shafi'i school, forgetting to connect a qualification makes it too late for divorce, emancipation, and other oaths.
rows.anchor: ومذهب الشافعي -رحمه الله-: أن الحالف إذا نسي الاستثناء موصولا بكلامه، فات وقته في الطلاق

rows.speaker: بعض أصحابنا
rows.claim: Some Shafi'i associates say it helps only if the person intended the qualification when starting the oath and then connected it; a later decision does not help.
rows.anchor: إنما ينفعه الاستثناء إذا أنشأ أول يمينه مع نية الاستثناء ثم وصله باليمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi's correct view is that a qualification benefits the swearer when it is connected to the oath.
rows.anchor: والصحيح: أنه إذا اتصل نفع، ووقع موقعه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report says one may qualify an oath whenever remembered, however much time has passed; al-Wahidi rejects it because a qualification must be attached to the speech it qualifies.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن عباس أنه قال: (يستثني الرجل في يمينه متى ما ذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse concerns a promise, not an oath: the Prophet had promised to answer about the Cave Companions the next day but had not sworn.
rows.anchor: والآية وردت في غير اليمين، وليس في الآية: ولا تحلفن على شيء إني فاعل ذلك غدا

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet said that one who swears and then sees a better course should take it and expiate the oath.
rows.anchor: من حلف على يمين ورأى غيرها خيرا منه، فليأت الذي هو خير ويكفر عن يمينه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If someone swears without intending an exception, the oath is established and cannot be undone by a later statement; a connected exception prevents it from becoming established.
rows.anchor: [فقد تمت يمينه واستقرت

rows.speaker: كثير من المفسرين
rows.claim: Many exegetes read “remember your Lord when you forget” as a new statement about something other than the qualification, which was already said in its proper connected place.
rows.anchor: لأن قوله: {واذكر ربك} ابتداء كلام آخر وقصة أخرى

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: “Remember your Lord when you forget” means when you become angry; remembering God removes anger caused by forgetting to remember Him.
rows.anchor: قال عكرمة: ({واذكر ربك إذا نسيت} قال: إذا غضبت)

rows.speaker: السدي والضحاك
rows.claim: The command concerns someone who forgets a prayer: he must pray it when he remembers.
rows.anchor: وروي عن السدي والضحاك أنهما قالا: (هذا فيمن نسي صلاة فعليه أن يصليها إذا ذكرها) (¬3)

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad says Ibn Abbas was too learned to let an unconnected qualification cancel an oath; his statement likely concerned a promise without an oath and was misreported as applying to oaths.
rows.anchor: إن ابن عباس أعلم من أن يسقط حكم الحنث بالاستثناء الذي لا يصله الحالف بيمينه

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: The Prophet asks to be guided to signs and proofs of prophethood clearer and more guiding than the story of the Cave Companions.
rows.anchor: أن يعطيني ربي من الآيات والدلالات على النبوة ما يكون أقرب في الرشد

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: God answered by giving the Prophet knowledge of messengers' unseen histories, clearer proof and guidance than the Cave story.
rows.anchor: حيث آتاه من علم غيوب المرسلين، وخبرهم ما كان أوضح في الحجة وأقرب إلى الرشد

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: The statement is to be said with the delayed qualification, as an expiation for forgetting it: the Prophet asks God to guide him so he will not forget again.
rows.anchor: هذا نبأ أمر أن يقوله مع الاستثناء إذا ذكر، وهو كفارة نسيان الاستثناء

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Alternatively, when the Prophet forgets something, he is told to remember God and ask to be reminded or guided to something better than what he forgot.
rows.anchor: هذا فيما ينساه النبي -صلى الله عليه وسلم- أمر أن يذكر الله تعالى فسأله أو يذكره ما نسي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس رواية الضحاك
rows.claim: The three-hundred-and-nine-year statement reports what the People of the Book said, not a direct report from God; its introductory “they will say” frames it as their claim.
rows.anchor: هذا إخبار عن أهل الكتاب أنهم قالوا ذلك

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada also says this is the People of the Book's claim, refuted by “God knows best”; Ibn Masud's reading explicitly says “they said they stayed.”
rows.anchor: هذا قول أهل الكتاب، فرد الله عليهم بقوله: {قل الله أعلم بما لبثوا}

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Ibn Masud's reading supports attributing the duration statement to the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: ويدل على صحة هذا قراءة ابن مسعود: قالوا لبثوا في كهفهم

rows.speaker: مطر الوراق
rows.claim: Matar al-Warraq gives the same interpretation: the duration is reported from the People of the Book.
rows.anchor: ونحو هذا قال مطر الوراق

rows.speaker: مجاهد، وعبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير، والضحاك
rows.claim: A second view takes the verse as God's own statement of the youths' stay from entering the cave until their resurrection and discovery.
rows.anchor: أن هذه الآية إخبار عن الله تعالى، أخبر عن قدر لبثهم في الكهف من يوم دخلوا

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj calls the interpretation that God is reporting their actual duration the strongest view; Ibn Qutayba also chooses it.
rows.anchor: واختاره الزجاج وقال: (هو الأجود عندي) (¬2)، وهو اختيار ابن قتيبة

rows.speaker: القتبي
rows.claim: On that view, God states the period and then says He knows better than those who differed about it.
rows.anchor: وأنا أعلم بما لبثوا من المختلفين

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: The Christians of Najran knew the three hundred years but not the additional nine, so “God knows best” was revealed in response.
rows.anchor: قالت نصارى نجران: أما الثلاثمائة فقد عرفناها، وأما التسع فلا علم لنا بها

rows.speaker: كثير من أهل التفسير
rows.claim: Another explanation says the People of the Book counted from the youths' entry until the Prophet's time; God replies that only He knows the period after their second death until the present.
rows.anchor: أن أهل الكتاب قالوا على رسول الله -صلى الله عليه وسلم-: أن الفتية من لدن دخلوا الكهف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس رواية عطاء
rows.claim: The first revelation said “three hundred” without a unit, leaving the Prophet unsure whether it meant years, months, days, or hours until Gabriel brought “years and nine more”; al-Dahhak and Muqatil report similarly.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية عطاء: (نزل قوله: {ولبثوا في كهفهم ثلاث مائة}

rows.speaker: ابن مجاهد
rows.claim: Because the words descended separately, Ibn Mujahid allowed a pause after “three hundred.”
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا أجاز ابن مجاهد الوقف على ثلاثمائة، لفصل ما بينهما في النزول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi prefers no pause: all grammarians attach “years” to “three hundred,” giving the sense “three hundred years”; “years” is an accusative complement of the verb.
rows.anchor: والاختيار ترك الوقف؛ لأن سنين وإن نزل بعد ثلاثمائة فقد التحق به في قول جميع النحويين

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: An alternative grammatical analysis makes “years” an appositional clarification or emphasis of “three.”
rows.anchor: ويجوز في تقدير العربية أن يكون سنين معطوفا على ثلاث، عطف البيان والتوكيد

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali parses “years” as a substitute for “three hundred,” with both words in the accusative.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو علي: {سنين} بدل من قوله: {ثلاث # مائة}

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra permits “years” as an accusative explanation of the number, comparing Antarah's “forty-two milk camels, black as a raven's wing.”
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون {سنين} نصبا بالتفسير للعدد، كما قال عنترة

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq allows “years” as an adjective of “hundred,” semantically describing the full counted number, like “black” describing the forty-two camels.
rows.anchor: وجائز أن يكون {سنين} من نعت المائة، وهو راجع في المعنى إلى ثلاث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi finds the adjectival analysis better than al-Farra's: “black” describes the camels and the full number, so “years” can describe “hundred” and the full number; on this reading it is genitive.
rows.anchor: وهذا القول أحسن من قول الفراء؛ لأنه جعل سودا تفسيرا للعدد، وليس كذلك تفسير العدد حلوبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He lists five possible parses for “years”: adverbial, appositional clarification, substitute, explanatory accusative, and adjective.
rows.anchor: وقد حصل في قوله: {سنين} خمسة أوجه من الإعراب: الظرف، وعطف البيان، والبدل، والتفسير، والنصت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common reading gives “hundred” nunation, while Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it in an unnunated construct with “years”; al-Wahidi calls that reading poor.
rows.anchor: وقراءة حمزة، والكسائي: "ثلاثمائة سنين" مضافة غير منونة

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن
rows.claim: Abu al-Hasan says Arabs rarely construct “a hundred” with the plural “years.”
rows.anchor: لا يحسن إضافة المائة إلى السنين، لا تكاد العرب تقول: مائة سنين

rows.speaker: صاحب النظم
rows.claim: The author of al-Nazm calls the construct reading strained when the number is stated explicitly.
rows.anchor: من أضاف وأظهر العدد اعتسف

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن
rows.claim: Abu al-Hasan nevertheless allows the construction and says some Arabs use it.
rows.anchor: إلا أن أبا الحسن قال: (هو جائز، وقد يقوله بعض العرب)

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says some Arabs use plural “years” where they mean a single year; in a construct, it is genitive.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: (من العرب من يضع السنين في موضع سنة

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: “They increased nine” cannot mean nine nights or hours: the previously stated counted unit, years, makes repeating the classifier unnecessary.
rows.anchor: لا يكون على معنى تسع ليال، ولا تسع ساعات؛ لأن العدد يعرف تفسيره

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: The phrase means they added nine years of stay; the verbal noun is omitted, and “nine” is an object rather than an adverbial of time.
rows.anchor: أي: ازدادوا لبث تسع، فحذف المصدر وأقيم المضاف إليه مقامه

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: “How perfectly He sees and hears!” is an exclamation, like “How generous Zayd is!”; if it were a command to a woman, it would take a different form.
rows.anchor: أي ما أبصره وأسمعه! كما تقول: أكرم به! أي ما أكرمه!

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: The referent is God: the construction means “How generous Abdullah is”; “how well they hear and see” in Maryam means the same kind of exclamation.
rows.anchor: يريد الله، كقولك: أكرم بعبد الله! ومعناه: ما أكرم عبد الله!

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Scholars agree that the phrase means “How well He hears and sees,” showing His knowledge of the Cave Companions and others.
rows.anchor: أجمع العلماء أن معناه: ما أسمعه وأبصره! أي: هو عالم بقصة أصحاب الكهف

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Arabic can use an imperative-shaped exclamation as a report and a report-shaped phrase as a prayer; the preposition and noun together occupy nominative position.
rows.anchor: العرب تتسع فتقيم المثال الذي يختص بالأمر مقام الخبر، والمثل المختص بالخبر موقع الدعاء والأمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The imperative-shaped expression has become a conventional exclamation, with no difference in meaning from “How excellent Zayd is!”
rows.anchor: ثم صار من ألفاظ التعجب حتى لا فصل بين قولك: ما أحسن زيدا! وقولك: أحسن بزيد

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The phrase means that God sees every existent and hears every audible thing; al-Wahidi says scholars agree on this exclamatory reading.
rows.anchor: ما أبصر الله بكل موجود، وأسمعه بكل مسموع

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd explains that God sees the deeds of those in the heavens and earth and hears them.
rows.anchor: معناه أنه يرى أعمال أهل السموات والأرض، ويسمع منهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس رواية عطاء
rows.claim: A minority reading takes this as a command: make God's friends see the Quran's marvels and hear through it; the object is omitted, but al-Wahidi says the established view is the exclamation.
rows.anchor: معناه أبصر أوليائي بعجائب القرآن، وأسمع به أوليائي

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: “They have no guardian besides Him” means the inhabitants of the heavens and earth have no protector besides God; the pronoun returns to those inhabitants mentioned in the preceding phrase.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: (أي ليس لأهل السموات والأرض من دون الله)

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Alternatively, the pronoun refers specifically to believers: having recognized God's majesty and lordship, they take no guardian besides Him.
rows.anchor: يريد قد عرفوا عظمتي وربوبيتي فلم يتخذوا من دوني وليا

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: “No one shares His judgment” can mean no one shares God's knowledge and power concerning the unseen, as in the Jinn verse, or that no judge may rule except by God's rulings and evidence from them.
rows.anchor: لا يشرك في حكمه بما يخبر به من الغيب أحدا كما قال: {عالم الغيب فلا يظهر على غيبه أحدا}

rows.speaker: ابن عامر
rows.claim: Ibn Amir reads “do not associate” as a prohibition addressed to a human against making anyone share God's judgment; it shifts from third person to direct address and echoes the idols verse.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عامر: ولا تشرك (¬2)، على معنى: ولا تشرك أنت أيها الإنسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common “He does not associate” reading fits better because the preceding clause has God as the absent third-person referent.
rows.anchor: والقراءة الأولى التي عليها العامة أشبه لتقدم اسم الغيبة

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: “Recite what was revealed” means follow the Quran.
rows.anchor: معناه: أتبع القرآن

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: “His words” refers to God's promises.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد لمواعيده)

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj explains the words as what God has foretold, which cannot be changed; the promise, ruling, and command are included.
rows.anchor: أي ما أخبر الله به، وما أخبر به فلا مبدل له

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi takes “His words” to mean the Quran, which no one can alter.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: (لا مغير للقرآن)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mujahid and al-Farra gloss mul tahad as refuge; al-Wahidi says refuge also derives from the notion of leaning toward something.
rows.anchor: ومن قال: ملجأ، فهو يؤول إلى هذا المعنى أيضا

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda glosses “mul tahad” as a place of turning aside.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: (معدلا)

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says there is no way to turn aside from God's commands and prohibitions.
rows.anchor: أي لن تجد معدلا عن أمره ونهيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root carries the sense of leaning: even seeking refuge means turning toward something; the same root appears in the verse about the tongue they incline to.
rows.anchor: وأصل هذا الحرف: من الميل، ومن قال: ملجأ، فهو يؤول إلى هذا المعنى أيضا

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says no refuge or protector can be found besides God.
rows.anchor: لا تجدون من دونه ملجأ ولا أحدا يمنعكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi refers readers to his fuller account of the occasion and variant reading under the passage in al-Anam.
rows.anchor: مفسرا بما فيه من النزول، واختلاف القراءة في سورة الأنعام

rows.speaker: علي عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: “Do not let your eyes pass beyond them” means do not look past them to others.
rows.anchor: يقول لا تتعداهم إلى غيرهم

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: The command means do not repel them with one's gaze or regard for others.
rows.anchor: يريد يصدهم بالنظر والمحبة لهم

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra glosses the phrase as “do not turn your eyes away from them.”
rows.anchor: لا تصرف عيناك عنهم

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says not to turn one's sight toward people of status and adornment; although the eyes are addressed, the Prophet is meant.
rows.anchor: لا تصرف بصرك إلى غيرهم من ذوي الهيئات والزينة

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The worldly adornment sought here means company with high-status and wealthy people.
rows.anchor: يعني مجالسة أهل الشرف والغنى

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: “Wanting worldly adornment” is a circumstantial phrase: the Prophet is forbidden to leave poor believers while seeking elite company.
rows.anchor: وقال أهل المعاني: (قوله: {تريد} هاهنا في موضع الحال)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet sought chiefs' faith hoping their followers would follow; he was not accused of worldly desire, but was directed to give believers his attention and not incline toward elites. Compare the rebuke in Abasa.
rows.anchor: وكان -صلى الله عليه وسلم- حريصا على إيمان الرؤساء طمعا في إيمان أتباعهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: “Do not obey the one whose heart We made heedless” refers to Uyaina and his father, who wanted the poor removed so they could sit with the Prophet.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد عيينة وأباهه) (¬1)، أي: لا تطعهم في تنحية الفقراء

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: “We made his heart heedless” can mean that God left him unmarked or found him heedless, like bare land or an unvowelled book.
rows.anchor: من جعلناه غافلا. قال: ويكون في الكلام أغفلته سميته غافلا، ووجدته غافلا

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid glosses “his affair was farat” as waste or loss.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: (ضياعا)

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says his affair was wasted in the greatest way.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: (ضاع أكبر الضيعة)

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi explains it as destruction.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: (هلاكا)

rows.speaker: أبو الهيثم
rows.claim: Abu al-Haytham takes “farat” as an affair treated carelessly; al-Wahidi connects this with neglect and ruin.
rows.anchor: أمر فرط، أي: متهاون به

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth says “farat” is an affair left unattended.
rows.anchor: الفرط: الأمر الذي يفرط فيه

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra explains “farat” as something left with obedience abandoned.
rows.anchor: فرطا: متروكا قد ترك فيه الطاعة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس رواية عطاء
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas via Ata says the man overreached in his demand and sought rank with God without piety; “farat” can derive from excess beyond bounds.
rows.anchor: يريد أنه أفرط في مسألته، وأحب أن يرتفع عند الله بغير تقوى

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil glosses the word as extravagance, which may mean the excessive demand described by Ibn Abbas or the neglect described by al-Kalbi and al-Farra.
rows.anchor: نحو هذا روي عن مقاتل أنه قال في قوله: {فرطا} قال: (سرفا)

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi reports Uyaina's boast that he and his people were Mudar's chiefs and that everyone would follow if they submitted.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: (قال عيينة: إنا رؤوس مضر (¬5) وأشرافها

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says Uyaina went too far by boasting that he was the Arabs' chief and they followed his religion, making his conduct excessive and boastful.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: (إنه أفرط في القول فقال: نحن رؤوس مضر وأشرافها، # وليس كذلك)

rows.speaker: أبو زيد البلخي
rows.claim: Abu Zayd al-Balkhi explains “farat” as a prior evil deed, from something that has gone ahead or occurred.
rows.anchor: معناه: قدما في الشر

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: The Prophet is to address people of every worldly rank who come to him.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء عن ابن عباس: (وقيل يا محمد # لمن جاءك من أهل الدنيا شريفا أو وضيعا)

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The addressees are those asking the Prophet to dismiss the poor and give them a closer seat so they might believe.
rows.anchor: قل لهؤلاء الذين أمروك بتنحية الفقراء عنك، وإدناء مجلسهم ليؤمنوا بك

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: “The truth is from your Lord” means Islam is the truth from your Lord.
rows.anchor: يعني هو الحق من ربكم، وهو الإسلام

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash supplies “it is”: say, “It is the truth.”
rows.anchor: أي قل: هو الحق

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق وقتادة
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq says the message brought to them is the truth; Qatada identifies it as the Quran.
rows.anchor: أي الذي أتيتكم به الحق من ربكم

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: “Whoever wills may believe and whoever wills may disbelieve” is a threat.
rows.anchor: قال السدي: (هذا على وجه الوعيد)

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says God has made the matter clear and then offered a choice, a choice intended as a threat.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: (إن ربكم بين ثم خير) (¬7)؛ يعني التخيير # الذي هو للتهديد

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj explains the apparent choice as warning, not a command whose alternatives would both count as obedience; the following verses specify each group's fate, the majority view.
rows.anchor: هذا الكلام ليس بأمر لهم ما فعلوا منه فهم فيه مطيعون، ولكنه كلام وعيد وإنذار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We have prepared” means made ready; “the wrongdoers” here are those who worship someone besides God.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {إنا أعتدنا} أي: هيأنا وأعددنا.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A saradiq is anything enclosing or surrounding something, such as cloth or a wall, and is most often used for a pavilion.
rows.anchor: معنى السرادق في اللغة: كل ما أحاط # بشيء واشتمل عليه من ثوب أو حائط

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth describes a saradiq as an enclosed chamber made from thick woven wool, used around royal pavilions.
rows.anchor: السرادق: كالحجرة المحوطة من غزل غليظ منسوج مضرب الأسفار للملوك

rows.speaker: رؤبة
rows.claim: Ru'ba's line uses “saradiq” for an expanse or canopy of glory spread over someone.
rows.anchor: سرادق المجد عليك ممدود

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azhari also uses the word for rising dust or conspicuous smoke surrounding something.
rows.anchor: ويقال للغبار الساطع، والدخان الشاخص المحيط بالشيء: سرادق

rows.speaker: لبيد
rows.claim: Labid applies “saradiq” to a covering raised around camels on a windy day.
rows.anchor: رفعن سرادقا في يوم ريح ... يصفق بين ميل واعتدال

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري عن النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet said Hell's enclosure has four walls, each wall a forty-year journey in thickness.
rows.anchor: روى أبو سعيد الخدري عن النبي -صلى الله عليه وسلم- قال: "سرادق النار أربع جدر

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi identifies the enclosure as smoke surrounding disbelievers on Judgment Day, and applies the same image to two other verses; Abu Ubayda and Ibn Qutayba choose this view.
rows.anchor: هو دخان يحيط بالكفار يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Those suffering will seek rescue from their punishment and intense thirst.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: أي مما هم فيه من العذاب وشدة العطش

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Abu Ubayd defines muhl as any smelted metal.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيد: (المهل: كل فلز (¬4) أذيب)

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: A report quotes Abu Bakr's instruction to bury him in two garments, saying they are for muhl and dust; Abu Ubayda interprets muhl there as pus and suppuration.
rows.anchor: ادفنوني # في ثوبي هذين، فإنما هما للمهل والتراب

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abu Amr says muhl in Abu Bakr's report means pus, while elsewhere it means sediment of oil.
rows.anchor: المهل في شيئين: هو في حديث أبي بكر: القيح والصديد، وفي غيره: دردي الزيت

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth calls muhl a kind of tar and gives a related verb for coating a camel with it.
rows.anchor: المهل: ضرب من القطران، يقال: مهلت البعير فهو ممهول

rows.speaker: ابن شميل عن شمر
rows.claim: Ibn Shumayl says muhl is like heated embers or clay when it becomes very hot and visibly waves.
rows.anchor: المهل عندهم الملة إذا حميت جدا رأيتها تموج

rows.speaker: العامرية
rows.claim: The Banu Amir dialect uses muhl for poison.
rows.anchor: وقالت العامرية: (المهل عندنا السم)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi counts six lexical senses of muhl.
rows.anchor: هذا معنى المهل في اللغة، وهو على ستة معان

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري عن النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet glossed the drink “like muhl” as the sediment of oil.
rows.anchor: روى أبو سعيد الخدري عن النبي -صلى الله عليه وسلم- في قوله: "بماء كالمهل" قال: "كعكر الزيت"

rows.speaker: ابن عباس رواية سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says it is oil sediment; al-Walibi and al-Awfi report similarly.
rows.anchor: وهو قول ابن عباس في رواية سعيد بن جبير قال: (كدردي الزيت)

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says muhl means pus and blood.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: "كالمهل" (القيح والدم)

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ata reports Ibn Abbas's interpretation as the sediment of tar.
rows.anchor: وقال عطاء عن ابن عباس: (هو عكر القطران)

rows.speaker: قتادة والحسن عن ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Asked about muhl, Ibn Masud melted gold and silver together and said the bubbling molten mixture was the closest worldly likeness of Hell's drink.
rows.anchor: أنه سئل عن المهل، فدعا بذهب وفضة فخلطهما، فأذيبا

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj chooses the molten-metal interpretation—lead, brass, or silver—because such metals reach extreme heat when melted.
rows.anchor: وهذا القول هو اختيار الزجاج فقال: (يعني أنهم # يغاثون بماء كالرصاص المذاب والصفر أو الفضة)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb for roasting meat is shawaytu; ashwaytu means roasting specifically for oneself, and inshawa and ishtawa are also used for being roasted.
rows.anchor: شويت اللحم أشويه شيا، فإذا شويته لنفسك خاصة قلت: أشويت

rows.speaker: لبيد
rows.claim: Labid's line uses a related form for roasting at night.
rows.anchor: فاشتوى ليلة ريح واجتمل

rows.speaker: الخدري عن النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet said that when the drink is brought close, the skin of the drinker's face falls into it.
rows.anchor: فإذا قربه إليه سقط فروة وجهه فيه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says it scorches the face until its flesh falls away.
rows.anchor: يشويه حتى يسقط لحم وجهه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “What a bad drink” refers to the water just described; “a bad resting place” describes Hell and is accusative as a specification.
rows.anchor: ثم ذمه فقال: {بئس الشراب} هذا الماء الذي وصفنا. {وساءت مرتفقا} أي: ساءت النار مرتفقا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The phrase means how bad the thing they rely on is.
rows.anchor: يريد وبئس ما ارتفقوا به

rows.speaker: مجاهد، وعطاء، والزجاج، وابن قتيبة
rows.claim: They gloss “resting place” as gathering, place, dwelling, or sitting place; al-Wahidi says these senses converge on a place where one finds use or comfort.
rows.anchor: فقال مجاهد: (مجتمعا) (¬4). وقال عطاء: (مقرا) (¬5). وقال الزجاج: (منزلا)

rows.speaker: ابن السكيت
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sikkit explains the word as a recliner, from leaning on one's elbow; a place where one stays and sits is a place of rest.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول ابن السكيت في قوله: {مرتفقا} قال: (متكأ)

rows.speaker: الهذلي
rows.claim: The Hudhali line “I slept at ease while lying on my elbow” supports the sense of reclining.
rows.anchor: نام الخلي وبت مرتفقا

rows.speaker: أهل اللغة
rows.claim: The common vocalization distinguishes thamar, meaning wealth, from thumur, meaning edible fruit; most exegetes take it as wealth here, while Ibn Zayd says it means the fruit-bearing trees themselves.
rows.anchor: فلأن أهل اللغة فرقوا بين الثمر والثمر # فقالوا: الثمر المال، والثمر المأكول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common reading is stronger because the owner turns his hands over what he spent on the garden, and spending usually goes to the productive trees and assets.
rows.anchor: وهذه القراءة أقوى الوجوه لقوله: {فأصبح يقلب كفيه على ما أنفق فيها}

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq prefers thamar because the earlier statement that both gardens yielded produce already establishes that meaning.
rows.anchor: الثمر هاهنا أحسن؛ لأن قوله: {كلتا الجنتين آتت أكلها} قد دل على الثمر

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abu Amr says both vocalized forms can denote kinds of wealth; the word here covers the garden, property, palms, and trees.
rows.anchor: وحكي عن أبي عمرو أنه قال: (الثمر والثمر أنواع المال) (¬3)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both readings can be clearer if they denote wealth and all the garden's assets; the reading in Asim's earlier clause as a particular crop is weak because that fruit was already implied, while the broad reading covers produce and roots.
rows.anchor: فمن قرأ: بثمره وثمره كان قوله أبين

rows.speaker: سلام أبو المنذر عن محمد بن سلام
rows.claim: Salam says one reading means all wealth and the other a plural of fruit; Yunus regards them as equivalent, but al-Wahidi rejects that conflation and preserves the distinction.
rows.anchor: وقال محمد بن سلام: (قال سلام أبو المنذر القارئ (¬1): من قرأ: "ثمر" قال: من كل المال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “If only, when you entered your garden” is a rebuke, equivalent to “Why did you not?”
rows.anchor: بمعنى: هلا، وتأويله التوبيخ

rows.speaker: الفراء والزجاج
rows.claim: One parse makes “what” a nominative subject: the matter is what God wills; this rebuts the unbelieving owner's claim that his garden would never perish.
rows.anchor: أنه في موضع رفع على معنى: الأمر ما شاء الله، أو: هو ما شاء الله

rows.speaker: الفراء والزجاج
rows.claim: Alternatively, “what” is the object of “wills” in a conditional phrase; the answer “whatever God wills occurs” is omitted but understood, as in the verse about seeking a tunnel through the earth.
rows.anchor: أن {ما} في موضع نصب ب (شاء) على معنى الشرط # والجزاء

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: No one can keep the property and blessing in his hands except through God, and a person has only what God wills.
rows.anchor: أي لا يقوى أحد على ما في يديه من ملك ونعمة إلا بالله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the believer then turned back to himself before saying he had less wealth and children.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (ثم رجع إلى نفسه) (¬3)

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: With “less” accusative, “I” is an emphatic separator; with “less” nominative, “I” is a noun; both readings are permissible.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: ({أنا} إذا نصبت {أقل} عماد، وإذا رفعت {أقل} فهي اسم

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: “I” can emphasize the attached first-person pronoun or serve as a separator; “less” can be accusative as the second object of “you see” or nominative as its subject's predicate.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو إسحاق بيانا فقال: ({أنا} يصلح لشيئين: إن شئت كانت توكيدا للنون والياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Its fruits were surrounded” means the punishment destroyed them, like an army encircling and wiping out an enemy.
rows.anchor: معنى "أحيط" هاهنا: أهلك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: “Its fruits” refers to the fruit trees and date palms.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (بأشجار الثمر والنخل) (¬5)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Turning the two palms means striking one hand against the other in regret.
rows.anchor: يضرب يديه واحدة على الأخرى ندامة

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi describes the gesture as clapping one hand against the other in regret.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: (يصفق بالواحدة على # الأخرى ندما)

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة والزجاج والمفضل وابن قتيبة
rows.claim: The phrase is an idiom for regret over what was lost: people turn their hands or palms as they reconsider a loss, much like biting one's hand; a poetic line illustrates the gesture.
rows.anchor: يقال: فلان يقلب كفيه على ما فاته، وتقليب الكفين يفعله النادم كثيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic can say one spent money “in” a house or garment, or “on” it; here “in” may mean “on,” as in the verse about crucifying people on palm trunks.
rows.anchor: فيجوز أن يكون هاهنا بمعنى: على، كقوله: {ولأصلبنكم في جذوع النخل}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The collapsed trellises include building roofs and vine frameworks: the structures lie fallen and empty of their trellised growth.
rows.anchor: والعروش في هذه الآية تعم سقوف الأبنية، وما عرش للكروم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The owner wishes he had not associated anyone with God, but the wish comes too late; God stripped his worldly blessings and his regret can no longer help.
rows.anchor: تمنى منه حين لا ينفعه التمني. أخبر الله تعالى أنه سلبه ما أنعم عليه

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: Calling God “better in reward” presumes hypothetically that anything else could endure; if it could, God's reward would still be better.
rows.anchor: قوله: {هو خير ثوابا} مع أنه لا يثبت إلا هو، على تقدير: لو كان يثبت غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that the wording answers the ignorant and disbelievers' supposition that something besides God might endure.
rows.anchor: وقيل: (هذا على ادعاء الجهال والكفار أنه قد يثبت غير الله)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Aqib” and “uqba” are forms for outcome; the ultimate outcome is not attributed to God as reward is, so the phrase means obedience to God has a better outcome than obedience to others, with “obedience” elided.
rows.anchor: ولا يجوز # أن يضاف العاقبة إلى الله تعالى أو يوصف بالعاقبة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The example is addressed to the Prophet's people.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد لقومك)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparison “like water” is a predicate of an omitted subject: worldly life is like water.
rows.anchor: الكاف في محل الرفع لخبر ابتداء محذوف، أي: هو كماء يعني: مثل الحياة الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The water sent down from heaven is rain.
rows.anchor: {كماء أنزلناه من السماء} يعني: المطر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “It mingled” means the vegetation entwined and gathered because of the water, since water makes plants grow abundantly.
rows.anchor: {فاختلط} فالتف واجتمع به، بذلك الماء أي: بسببه

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq says the water penetrates the plants until they become lush; the plant is mixed with the water by being watered.
rows.anchor: تأويله أنه نجع في النبات حتى خالطه، فأخذ النبات زخرفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plant becomes hasheem: brittle, broken vegetation; the word derives from breaking, as in breaking bread, and is related to the name Hashim.
rows.anchor: معنى الهشم في اللغة: الكسر، والهاشم: الذي يهشم الخبز ويكسره في الثريد

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Exegetes describe hasheem as broken and crumbled vegetation.
rows.anchor: أنه الكسير المتفتت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The winds scatter it” means wind carries an object, raises it, and stirs it; the verb has several dialect forms, and Ibn Masud reads “tudhrihi.”
rows.anchor: الذر حمل الريح الشيء ثم تثيره، يقال: ذرته الريح، تذروه، وتذريه

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The phrase means the winds lift, disperse, and blow the vegetation away.
rows.anchor: ترفعه وتفرقه وتنسفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This image is a shortened version of the water-and-vegetation example in Yunus, which al-Wahidi explains there in detail.
rows.anchor: وهذه الآية مختصرة من قوله في سورة يونس: {إنما مثل الحياة الدنيا كماء أنزلناه من السماء}

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says God teaches that worldly life passes away, using this comparison.
rows.anchor: أعلم الله أن الحياة الدنيا زائلة، وأن مثلها هذا المثل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is capable of creating and ending everything: He brought vegetation into existence and then made it perish.
rows.anchor: على كل شيء من الإنشاء والإفناء قادرا، أنشأ النبات ولم يكن، ثم أفناه

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan says God was able to bring every thing into being before it existed.
rows.anchor: كان الله على كل شيء مقتدرا أن يكونه قبل كونه

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says grammarians understand “was able” as “has always been able”; the power people witness is not newly acquired by God.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج وهو مذهب # النحويين في هذا: (أن معناه كان مقتدرا لم يزل)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question asks about people whose deeds make them the greatest losers among creation.
rows.anchor: أي: بالقوم الذين هم أخسر الخلق فيما عملوا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس رواية عطاء
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies them as disbelieving People of the Book.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية عطاء: (يرد كفار أهل الكتاب)

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi identifies them as Jews and Christians.
rows.anchor: وهو قول الكلبي: (اليهود والنصارى)

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: One report from Ali identifies them as monks living in cells.
rows.anchor: وروي عن علي -رضي الله عنه- أنه قال: (هم الرهبان أصحاب الصوامع) (¬6)

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Another report from Ali identifies them as the people of Harura, the Kharijites.
rows.anchor: وعنه أيضا أنه قال: (هم أهل حروراء) (¬1)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Those whose striving went astray” can be genitive as an adjective of “the greatest losers,” or nominative as a fresh sentence meaning “they are those.”
rows.anchor: يجوز في {الذين} الخفض بالنعت للأخسرين. ويجوز الرفع على الاستيئناف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their effort and work in worldly life were fruitless, though they believed they were doing well.
rows.anchor: بطل عملهم واجتهادهم في الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Sunʿ” is the verbal noun of doing a favor and is most often used for good works.
rows.anchor: والصنع: مصدر صنع إليه معروفا يصنع صنعا، وأكثر ما يستعمل الصنع في الأعمال الحسنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God creates mutual love among believers so they love, show mercy to, and feel affection for one another.
rows.anchor: أي: يجعلهم يحب بعضهم بعضا، فيتراحمون ويتعاطفون بما جعل الله لبعضهم في قلوب بعض

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: God loves them and makes believers love them; Mujahid and Qatada say similarly.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يحبهم ويحببهم إلى المؤمنين) (¬3)

rows.speaker: هرم بن حيان
rows.claim: When a servant turns his heart toward God, God turns believers' hearts toward him and grants their affection, love, and mercy.
rows.anchor: ما أقبل عبد بقلبه إلى الله إلا أقبل الله بقلوب المؤمنين إليه

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say God first places love for them in angels' hearts and then in people's hearts.
rows.anchor: يجعل لهم في قلوب الملائكة ودا ثم في قلوب العباد

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة عن النبي
rows.claim: A prophetic report says when God loves a servant, He tells Gabriel to love him, announces this in heaven, and love then descends among earth's people.
rows.anchor: إذا أحب الله عبدا نادى جبريل إني قد أحببت فلانا فأحبه

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: The verse was revealed about Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, whom God made beloved: believers honored him, and even disbelievers and hypocrites treated him with respect.
rows.anchor: نزلت الآية في عبد الرحمن بن عوف جعل الله له في قلوب العباد المودة

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: The singular “one” is named while the plural is meant, including anyone who acts and bears the same qualities and shares the good reward.
rows.anchor: سمي الواحد باسم الجمع لدخول من فعل مثل فعله في مثل وصفه وحسن جزائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is told to endure what people say until God rules; then He decreed their killing, ending the command to endure their abuse.
rows.anchor: أمره بالصبر إلى أن يحكم الله، ثم حكم فيهم بالقتل، فنسخ الصبر على ما يسمع من أذاهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Glorify with praise” means perform prayer while praising and extolling God.
rows.anchor: {وسبح بحمد ربك} صل لله بالحمد له والثناء عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Before sunrise refers to dawn prayer; before sunset refers to afternoon prayer.
rows.anchor: {قبل طلوع الشمس} يريد: الفجر {وقبل غروبها} يريد: العصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Hours of the night” means its times; the singular forms and two poetic lines illustrate the word's usage.
rows.anchor: ساعاته واحدها إني مثل: نحي وأنحاء

rows.speaker: الأعشى
rows.claim: Al-Asha's line uses ini for a span or time of night.
rows.anchor: بكل إني قضاه الليل ينتعل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the early night prayers as Maghrib and Isha.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد أول الليل المغرب والعشاء)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس رواية عطاء، مجاهد، قتادة
rows.claim: They identify “the edges of the day” as the noon prayer; noon is the boundary between the day's two halves, and a dual can be called a plural.
rows.anchor: {فسبح وأطراف النهار} يريد: الظهر. هذا الذي ذكرنا في تفسير هذه الآية

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra gives the same interpretation of “the edges of the day” as noon prayer.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول الفراء في هذه الآية

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: Abu al-Abbas says the plural refers to the two edges recurring each day.
rows.anchor: جمع الطرفين؛ لأنه يلزم في كل نهار يعود

rows.speaker: بعض المفسرين
rows.claim: Some exegetes take the edges to mean morning and evening, inferred from the preceding dawn and sunset phrases.
rows.anchor: ومن المفسرين من حمل أطراف النهار على: الغدوة والعشية

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi says the edges of the day are its hours.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأعرابي: (أطراف النهار: ساعاته) (¬7)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: “So that you may be pleased” means God guarantees the Prophet's reward and final return.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: (يريد: الثواب # والمعاد واجبا من الله لك)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb has readings with a damma or fatha on its initial ta; the open reading is supported by the promise that God will give until the Prophet is satisfied.
rows.anchor: وفيه قراءتان: ضم التاء وفتحها (¬2). فمن فتح التاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the damma reading, the meaning can be that the Prophet is pleased by performing God's approved commands or by receiving a high rank.
rows.anchor: ويكون المعنى لعلك ترضى بفعل ما أمرك به من الأفعال التي يرضاها الله

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Abu Ubayd chooses the damma reading because it allows both being granted contentment and God's being pleased, supported by the description of Moses as pleasing to his Lord.
rows.anchor: واختار أبو عبيد هذه القراءة لاحتمالها معنيين أحدهما: ترضى: تعطى الرضى، والآخر: يرضاك الله

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: One grammatical analysis makes “that” the subject and “because of what your hands sent ahead” its predicate; “and because God is not unjust” is genitive after the preposition.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: المعنى: يقال له هذا العذاب بما قدمت يداك

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Alternatively, “that” is a predicate with an omitted “the matter”; the clause about God's justice is then nominative as another predicate.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون موضع "ذلك" رفعا على خبر الابتداء

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali rejects making “that” a predicate because this leaves the prepositional phrase unattached; he treats the “that God” clause as genitive coordination, as in the parallel verse.
rows.anchor: وأبطل أبو علي أن يكون "ذلك" خبر الابتداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Wahidi refers the interpretation of this verse to his discussion of the parallel wording in al-Anfal.
rows.anchor: وأما معنى هذه الآية فهو مما ذكرناه في سورة الأنفال عند قوله

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Most exegetes understand worshipping God “on an edge” as worship based on doubt.
rows.anchor: أكثر المفسرين على أن المعنى: على شك

rows.speaker: مجاهد، والسدي، وقتادة، وأبو إسحاق، وأبو زيد، وابن الأعرابي
rows.claim: These authorities take “on an edge” to mean in doubt; al-Wahidi distinguishes this as the contextual meaning rather than the word's literal lexical sense.
rows.anchor: وهو قول مجاهد (¬1) والسدي وقتادة (¬2)، واختيار أبي إسحاق (¬3) وأبي زيد وابن الأعرابي

rows.speaker: ابن اليزيدي عن أبي زيد
rows.claim: Abu Zayd glosses the phrase as doubt.
rows.anchor: روى ابن اليزيدي (¬4) عن أبي زيد: على حرف على شك

rows.speaker: ابن الأعرابي وأحمد بن يحيى
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi and Ahmad ibn Yahya also explain the phrase as doubt.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأعرابي: [الحرف] (¬6) الشك في قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The literal lexical meaning of harf is an edge, end, side, or margin; the word for deviation also means turning toward a side.
rows.anchor: وتفسير الحرف في اللغة: الطرف وهو منتهى الجسم، والحرف والطرف والجانب نظائر في اللغة

rows.speaker: أبو الفتح الموصلي
rows.claim: Abu al-Fath says the root h-r-f conveys a boundary or sharpness: an object's edge is its limit or side, and food called harif is pungent.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو الفتح الموصلي: أما الحرف فالقول فيه أن (ح ر ف)

rows.speaker: أبو الفتح الموصلي
rows.claim: He explains “turned away from me” as setting a boundary through distance, and the pungent plant as named for its sharpness.
rows.anchor: انحرف فلان عني، من هذا، كأنه جعل بيني وبينه حدا بالبعد والاعتزال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One etymology derives edge from inclination away from the center; Abu al-Fath instead derives it from sharpness.
rows.anchor: وعلى القول الأول أصل الحرف من الميل سمي الطرف حرفا

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: The worshipper stands on the edge of religion's path without entering it as someone firmly settled.
rows.anchor: وحقيقته أنه يعبد الله على حرف الطريقة في الدين، لا يدخل فيه دخول متمكن

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda says the person does not persevere; saying someone is “on an edge” means he cannot be trusted.
rows.anchor: أي لا يدوم. قال: وتقول (¬4): إنما أنت على حرف

rows.speaker: أبو الفتح
rows.claim: This returns to instability: the doubter stands at the edge of faith like someone on a cliff, ready to fall at the slightest disturbance; firm belief would not waver.
rows.anchor: قال أبو الفتح: وهذا راجع إلى ما قدمناه لأن تأويله أنه قلق

rows.speaker: بعض أهل المعاني
rows.claim: Some say doubt arises from weakness and lack of mastery of the proofs: a slight objection leads the person astray instead of being resolved.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض أهل المعاني: إنما قيل للشاك في دينه: يعبد الله على حرف

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad says a person “on an edge” may show a preference for one group while privately harboring reservations about another; the image is an unstable boundary or footing.
rows.anchor: فلان على حرف، إذا كان بين قوم يظهر الميل إلى أحدهم وفي نفسه من الآخرين شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These explanations all return to the same underlying idea.
rows.anchor: هذا الذي ذكرناه كله يعود إلى معنى واحد

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba takes “one edge” to mean one aspect, one way, or one school of thought.
rows.anchor: وقال (¬2) ابن قتيبة: {ومن الناس من يعبد الله على حرف}

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azhari prefers the one-sided-worship interpretation: prosperity is one side and adversity another, and a servant should worship the Creator in both.
rows.anchor: اختار الأزهري هذا القول فقال: كأن الخير والخصب ناحية، والضر والشر والمكروه ناحية أخرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On this view, someone who worships only in prosperity is on one edge, while worship in both ease and hardship shows acceptance of the Creator's direction.
rows.anchor: ومن عبد الله على السراء وحدها دون أن # يعبده على الضراء فقد عبده على حرف

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan identifies the person as a hypocrite who worships with his tongue but not his heart; “on an edge” then means doubt.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: هو المنافق يعبد الله بلسانه دون قلبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The good that brings reassurance means prosperity, health, abundant crops, and wealth; the pronoun in “he is reassured by it” refers to that good.
rows.anchor: قوله: {فإن أصابه خير اطمأن به} إن أصابه رخاء (¬5) وعافية وخصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The trial means drought and loss of wealth.
rows.anchor: اختبار بجدب وقلة مال

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: To turn on one's face means to leave religion for disbelief and idol worship.
rows.anchor: رجع عن دينه إلى الكفر وعبادة الأوثان

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad says he turns away from the religion he had followed; “face” may mean the path from which he came, namely disbelief.
rows.anchor: قلب وجهه عما كان عليه من الدين والعبادة

rows.speaker: الكلبي وغيره من المفسرين
rows.claim: The verse was revealed about Bedouins who came to Medina: prosperity made one praise the faith, but illness, loss, or delayed charity led Satan to make him renounce it.
rows.anchor: نزلت في أعراب كانوا يقدمون على رسول الله -صلى الله عليه وسلم- المدينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wavering worshipper loses worldly life by failing to obtain the wealth he sought and the afterlife by apostasy; this is the manifest loss.
rows.anchor: خسر دنياه حيث لم يظفر بما طلب من المال، وخسر آخرته بارتداده عن الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb “he lost” itself indicates the noun “loss.”
rows.anchor: وخسر يدل على الخسران؛ لأن الفعل يدل على المصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who denied resurrection ask to return to worldly life when they see death approaching.
rows.anchor: أن هؤلاء الذين ذكروا قبل هذا الموضع ودفعوا البعث يسألون المرجع إلى الدنيا

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says the person who asks to return is a disbeliever.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: يعني (¬3) الكفار

rows.speaker: الكلبي ومقاتل
rows.claim: They explain “death came” as meaning the Angel of Death came.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي ومقاتل (¬5): يعني ملك الموت

rows.speaker: غيرهما
rows.claim: Others take “death” to mean its causes and early signs, as in the verse about death coming from every direction.
rows.anchor: وقال غيرهما: يعني (¬6) أسباب الموت ومقدماته

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والمفسرون
rows.claim: “My Lord, send me back” means return me to worldly life.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس والمفسرون: يريد إلى الدنيا

rows.speaker: الفراء والزجاج وجميع أصحاب العربية
rows.claim: The plural imperative “send me back” addresses God alone; Arabic uses a plural form for a majestic speaker, as in God's “We give life and cause death.”
rows.anchor: قال الفراء، والزجاج، وجميع أصحاب العربية: قوله: {ارجعون} وهو يريد الله -عز وجل- وحده

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says the dying person first calls on God and then turns to the angels to ask for return.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن جريج أنه قال -في هذه الآية-: إنهم استغاثوا

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad chooses the angels as the addressees of “send me back,” after the person first appeals to God; Arabic can shift addressees mid-speech, as in lines by al-Ahwas and al-Nabigha addressing a house before its owner.
rows.anchor: واختار المبرد هذا الوجه فقال: {ارجعون} خطاب للملائكة بعد أن قال: رب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The righteous deed the dying person hopes to perform is bearing witness that there is no god but God.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد أشهد أن لا إله إلا الله

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says the hoped-for righteous action means faith.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: يعني الإيمان

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the disbeliever did not wish to return to family or tribe, only to obey God; the living should take heed of that wish.
rows.anchor: ما تمنى أن يرجع إلى أهل ولا عشيرة، ولكنه تمنى أن يرجع فيعمل بطاعة الله

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: “In what I left behind” means the time already passed in his life.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: فيما مضى من عمري

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi explains it as the things the person denied.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: فيما كذبت

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Another interpreter says it means what he neglected.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره: فيما ضيعت

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: “Never!” means he will not return to worldly life; the request is inevitably spoken at death when he sees God's punishment, as Ibn Zayd also says.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يقول لا ترجع إلى الدنيا {إنها}

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Others say the request is only empty speech: it brings no benefit because the speaker will not receive what he asks, like the two verses about saying things with one's mouth.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون (¬1): {كلمة هو قائلها} يعني أن سؤاله الرجعة كلام يقوله

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda says “behind them” means ahead of them.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة: ومن أمامهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase can mean between them as Abu Ubayda says, or behind them as in the earlier reference to Hell behind a person.
rows.anchor: ومن بين أيديهم، كما قال أبو عبيدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Barzakh literally means any barrier between two things, concrete or abstract, such as distance, a wall, days, or hostility.
rows.anchor: معنى البرزخ في اللغة: الحاجز بين الشيئين

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra says barzakh, barrier, and interval are close in meaning; the obstacle may be distance or something that prevents an event.
rows.anchor: وهذا معنى قول الفراء، قال: البرزخ والحاجز والمهلة

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: A report says Ali omitted a barzakh during prayer, meaning the interval between the position he left and the position where he ended up.
rows.anchor: أنه صلى بقوم فأسوى (¬3) برزخا (¬4). أي أسقط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word also describes the boundary between certainty and doubt; a dead person is in barzakh because he lies between worldly life and the next life.
rows.anchor: وبرازخ الإيمان ما بين اليقين والشك

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq defines the barzakh here as the barrier between a person's death and resurrection; al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd say similarly.
rows.anchor: البرزخ في اللغة: الحاجز، وهو هاهنا ما بين موت الميت وبعثه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains barzakh as a veil.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن عباس: ([برزخ]: حجاب

rows.speaker: السدي ومقاتل
rows.claim: Al-Suddi and Muqatil gloss barzakh as a fixed term or appointed span.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي ومقاتل: أجل

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says it is a veil preventing their return to worldly life until resurrection.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: حجاب بينهم وبين (¬5) الرجوع إلى الدنيا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says it is the remainder of worldly life: they stay in barzakh until the world ends and they are resurrected.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: بقية الدنيا (¬7)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “behind them is a barzakh” refers to the same people as the preceding phrase “when one of them is reached by death.”
rows.anchor: والكناية (¬9) في قوله: {ومن ورائهم برزخ} كالكناية

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: The time noun “day” is annexed to the verb “they are resurrected,” since Arabic permits temporal nouns to be annexed to verbs.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق: {يوم} مضاف إلى
